learningObjective: Explain why the Halide paper separates the algorithm (what to compute) from the schedule (how to compute) and identify the design intent behind this separation.
stem: The Halide paper is best known for separating the algorithm (what to compute) from the schedule (how to compute). Which statement best captures the design intent argued in the paper?

options.text: The separation exists so that the compiler can hide the algorithm behind an opaque API; users interact only with schedules.

The separation lets a single, portable algorithm be re-scheduled (tiled, vectorized, parallelized, fused, recomputed) without changing its semantics, so many performance-relevant strategies can be explored on each target without rewriting the pipeline.
The separation is required for correctness: only by moving loop order out of the algorithm can Halide guarantee that per-pixel updates remain race-free on multi-core CPUs.
The separation is a legacy artifact from Halide's origins as a C++ template library; in modern implementations the two parts are merged and the design contribution is largely obsolete.

explanation: Halide's §1–§3 explicitly argue that the algorithm/schedule split is the central design contribution: the algorithm is a portable, semantics-only description; the schedule expresses per-target loop nesting, tiling, parallelization and storage/recomputation trade-offs. Users can enumerate many schedules cheaply, autotuners can search over them, and the compiler guarantees each legal schedule preserves the algorithm's output.

optionExplanations.A: Wrong: the paper argues for exposing schedules to programmers, not hiding algorithms.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: matches the paper's stated design intent — portability + tunability without rewriting.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: correctness is preserved by dependence analysis, not by the syntactic separation itself.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: the separation is Halide's flagship contribution, not a legacy artifact.

assumptions: Understanding that a 'schedule' in Halide covers loop order, tiling, storage, parallel/vector directives, and produce-consume relations.
nonImplications: Does not imply that any schedule is beneficial; most are worse than the default.
Does not imply Halide's schedule language is complete for every optimization; some transformations (e.g. arbitrary polyhedral reordering) fall outside its scope.

distractorRationales.C: Confuses dependence analysis with algorithm/schedule separation.
